Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Continuity is as in [[def-continuous-map-top]],
injections, surjections and bijections as in
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]].

- $f$ is an **open map** if $f[U]$ is open in $Y$ for every open $U \subseteq X$.
- $f$ is a **closed map** if $f[F]$ is closed in $Y$ for every closed
  $F \subseteq X$.
- $f$ is a **homeomorphism** if $f$ is a continuous bijection whose inverse
  $f^{-1} : Y \to X$ is also continuous. The spaces are **homeomorphic**, written
  $X \cong Y$, when a homeomorphism $X \to Y$ exists.
- $f$ is an **embedding** if $f$ is injective and the corestriction
  $f_0 : X \to f[X]$, $f_0(x) = f(x)$, is a homeomorphism onto $f[X]$ carrying
  the subspace topology inherited from $Y$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**The inverse in the third clause exists because $f$ is a bijection**, and it is
the unique two-sided inverse ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); no choice
principle is involved. Continuity of $f^{-1}$ is a genuine additional demand: a
continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism, and this page records that
failure as a false statement with a two-point witness.

**Open, closed and homeomorphism are three different conditions.** A
homeomorphism is continuous by definition, but an open map need not be continuous
and a closed map need not be continuous; and continuity implies neither openness
nor closedness. An open map need
not be closed and a closed map need not be open, and Sierpinski space
$S = \{a,b\}$ with open point $b$ ([[def-standard-topologies]]) witnesses both
failures at once: the constant map $S \to S$ with value $b$ is open, since the
image of every nonempty set is the open set $\{b\}$, and is not closed, since the
image of the closed set $\{a\}$ is $\{b\}$, whose complement $\{a\}$ is not open;
the constant map with value $a$ is closed and not open by the same computation
read the other way. What is true
is that for a **continuous bijection** the three notions collapse: it is a
homeomorphism exactly when it is open, exactly when it is closed. That is proved
in the next item and is not assumed here.

**Topological properties.** A **property of topological spaces** is a condition
$P$ that is either true or false of each space. $P$ is a **topological property**
(one is also said to be *preserved by homeomorphism*, or *invariant*) when
$X \cong Y$ implies that $P(X)$ and $P(Y)$ have the same truth value. Since
$\cong$ is an equivalence relation on spaces — the identity is a homeomorphism,
inverses and composites of homeomorphisms are homeomorphisms, all three verified
in the next item — a topological property is exactly one that is constant on each
$\cong$-class.

**What a homeomorphism transports.** If $h : X \to Y$ is a homeomorphism then
$U \mapsto h[U]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{T}_X$ onto $\mathcal{T}_Y$, with
inverse $V \mapsto h^{-1}[V]$: both maps are well defined because $h$ and
$h^{-1}$ are continuous, and they are mutually inverse because $h$ is a
bijection. So a homeomorphism is an isomorphism of the structure "a set together
with a distinguished family of subsets", and every notion defined from the open
sets alone — closed, closure, interior, boundary, dense, convergence of
sequences, continuity of maps into and out of the space — is carried across by
it. Anything defined from extra data, such as a metric or an order, is not, and
that distinction is exactly what the phrase *topological property* is for.

Let $X$ be a set and write $\mathcal{P}(X)$ for its power set. A **topology** on
$X$ is a family $\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ such that

- **(T1)** $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}$ and $X \in \mathcal{T}$;
- **(T2)** $\bigcup \mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{T}$ for every $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$;
- **(T3)** $U \cap V \in \mathcal{T}$ for all $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$.

A **topological space** is a pair $(X, \mathcal{T})$ consisting of a set $X$ and
a topology $\mathcal{T}$ on it; the elements of $X$ are its **points**. When only
one topology is in play we write $X$ for the pair; when several are, the topology
is always named.

The members of $\mathcal{T}$ are the **open** sets of $(X,\mathcal{T})$. A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed** when its complement $X \setminus F$ is open, and
**clopen** when it is both open and closed. By (T1) both $\varnothing$ and $X$
are clopen. *Open and closed are not opposites*: a set may be neither, and it may
be both, so "not open" is never a synonym for "closed".

**Finite intersections, and the empty one.** Axiom (T3) is stated for two sets
because that is all that is ever needed: if $n \ge 1$ and
$U_1, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{T}$, then $U_1 \cap \dots \cap U_n \in \mathcal{T}$
follows by iterating (T3) $n-1$ times. The intersection of the **empty** family
of subsets of $X$ is $X$, since the condition "lies in every member of the empty
family" is vacuous; that case is covered by (T1) rather than by (T3), which is
one of the two reasons $X \in \mathcal{T}$ is demanded outright. The other is
that (T2) alone gives only $\bigcup \varnothing = \varnothing$.

**The closed sets, and the dual axiomatisation.** Put
$\mathcal{C} := \{\, X \setminus U : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\}$, the family of closed
sets. Then

- **(C1)** $\varnothing \in \mathcal{C}$ and $X \in \mathcal{C}$;
- **(C2)** $\bigcap \mathcal{D} \in \mathcal{C}$ for every **nonempty**
  $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$;
- **(C3)** $C \cup D \in \mathcal{C}$ for all $C, D \in \mathcal{C}$.

Conversely, if a family $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ satisfies (C1),
(C2) and (C3), then $\mathcal{T} := \{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{C} \,\}$
is a topology on $X$ whose closed sets are exactly the members of $\mathcal{C}$.
So a topology may be presented equally well by its open sets or by its closed
sets, and this library uses whichever is shorter.

*Both directions are one computation, and it is carried out here rather than
assumed.* The map $U \mapsto X \setminus U$ is an involution of
$\mathcal{P}(X)$, hence a bijection, and it carries the two De Morgan identities

$$X \setminus \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcap_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad (I \ne \varnothing), \qquad X \setminus \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcup_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad (I \ne \varnothing)$$

term by term into each other. Given (T1)–(T3): $\varnothing = X \setminus X$ and
$X = X \setminus \varnothing$ lie in $\mathcal{C}$, which is (C1); for nonempty
$\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ the family
$\mathcal{S} = \{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{D} \,\}$ lies in $\mathcal{T}$
and $\bigcap \mathcal{D} = X \setminus \bigcup \mathcal{S}$ is closed by (T2),
which is (C2); and $C \cup D = X \setminus ((X \setminus C) \cap (X \setminus D))$
is closed by (T3), which is (C3). Given (C1)–(C3) the same three lines run
backwards, the empty-union case $\bigcup \varnothing = \varnothing$ being supplied
by (C1) rather than by (C2); and $\{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{C} \,\}$ has
$\mathcal{C}$ as its family of complements because complementation is an
involution.

**Comparison of topologies.** If $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ are
topologies on the same set $X$ and $\mathcal{T}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_2$, then
$\mathcal{T}_1$ is **coarser** than $\mathcal{T}_2$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ is
**finer** than $\mathcal{T}_1$; the comparison is **strict** when the inclusion
is. Inclusion is a partial order on the set of topologies on $X$
([[def-partial-order]]), and it is not a total one: two topologies on the same
set may be incomparable.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$. For $n\ge1$, put $\mathbb R^n:=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb R$ with its
usual topology; for $n=0$ put $\mathbb R^0:=\{0\}$, the one-point space. A
**topological $n$-manifold without boundary** (or briefly an **$n$-manifold**) is
a topological space $M$ satisfying:

1. $M$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]);
2. $M$ is second countable ([[def-second-countable-space]]);
3. $M$ is **locally Euclidean of dimension $n$**: every $p\in M$ has an open
   neighbourhood $U\subseteq M$ homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

The empty space satisfies all three conditions vacuously, so $M=\varnothing$ is
an $n$-manifold for every $n$; this degenerate instance is kept, and statements
about nonempty manifolds name the hypothesis. In dimension zero, condition 3
forces the one-point neighbourhoods of points to be open singletons, so a
$0$-manifold is exactly a discrete second-countable space with at most countably
many points.

A topological space $(X, \mathcal{T})$ ([[def-topological-space]]) is
**Hausdorff** when any two distinct points are separated by disjoint open sets:
for all $x, y \in X$ with $x \ne y$ there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with

$$x \in U, \qquad y \in V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$

Since an open set containing a point is an open neighbourhood of it
([[def-neighbourhood-top]]), the condition reads: distinct points have disjoint
open neighbourhoods. Nothing is asserted about points that are equal, and the
condition is vacuous for a space with at most one point, so every such space is
Hausdorff.

**Every metrizable space is Hausdorff.** This is not proved here, because it is
already discharged: [[def-metrizable-space]] records it among the two things
every metrizable space has, deriving it from
[[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], which separates $p \ne q$ in a metric space
by the disjoint open balls $B(p,r)$ and $B(q,r)$ with $r = d(p,q)/2 > 0$. In
particular $\mathbb{R}$ with its usual topology, every $\mathbb{R}^n$, and every
subspace of a metrizable space are Hausdorff.

**Not every space is Hausdorff.** The indiscrete topology
$\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{ind}} = \{\varnothing, X\}$ on a set $X = \{a,b\}$ with
$a \ne b$ ([[def-standard-topologies]]) is not: the only open set containing $a$
is $X$, the only one containing $b$ is $X$, and $X \cap X = X \ne \varnothing$.
This is the same two-point space that [[def-metrizable-space]] uses to exhibit a
topology induced by no metric, and the reason is the same one: failure of the
Hausdorff condition is an obstruction to metrizability.

**Being Hausdorff is a topological property** ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).
If $h : X \to Z$ is a homeomorphism and $X$ is Hausdorff, then for $z \ne z'$ in
$Z$ the points $h^{-1}(z)$ and $h^{-1}(z')$ are distinct, so they have disjoint
open $U, V$; the images $h[U]$ and $h[V]$ are open, disjoint, and contain $z$ and
$z'$ respectively, a homeomorphism carrying the open sets of one space
bijectively onto those of the other. So no space homeomorphic to a Hausdorff
space fails the condition.

**Scope of this item.** Only the definition, the metrizable case and the
two-point failure are recorded here, because that is all this page uses. The
Hausdorff condition is one of a graded family of separation axioms; that family,
its ordering, and the questions of which of its members are hereditary or
preserved by products, are not available at this point in the reading order and
nothing here anticipates them. What this page does use is a single negative
result: a quotient of a Hausdorff space need not be Hausdorff, which is recorded
below as a false statement and witnessed on the companion page.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $p, q \in X$ with
$p \ne q$. Put $r := d(p,q)/2$. Then $r > 0$ and

$$B(p,r) \cap B(q,r) = \emptyset .$$

Both sets are open ([[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]) and contain $p$
respectively $q$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), so every metric space is **Hausdorff**:
distinct points are separated by disjoint open sets
([[def-metric-topology]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, and give $\mathbb{R}$ its usual topology,
the metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metrizable-space]]). Let

$$\mathbb{R}^n \;=\; \prod_{k < n} \mathbb{R}$$

be the product of $n$ copies of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-product-topology]]). As a
**set** this is literally the $\mathbb{R}^n$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], both being
the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$; and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are the
three metrics defined there. Then:

1. The product topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the metric topology of $d_\infty$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]). The key computation is that a $d_\infty$-ball is a
   box:
   $$B_{d_\infty}(x, r) \;=\; \prod_{k<n} (x_k - r,\ x_k + r) \qquad (r > 0),$$
   a product of bounded open intervals ([[def-interval]]).
2. $d_\infty \le d_1 \le n\, d_\infty$ and $d_\infty \le d_2 \le n\, d_\infty$
   pointwise, so $d_1$ and $d_2$ are each Lipschitz equivalent to $d_\infty$
   ([[def-equivalent-metrics]]); here $n$ denotes the canonical natural
   $n \cdot 1_{\mathbb{R}}$.
3. Consequently all three metrics induce the product topology
   ([[thm-metric-equivalence-hierarchy]]). So $\mathbb{R}^n$ carrying the product
   topology and $\mathbb{R}^n$ carrying the topology of any one of $d_1$, $d_2$,
   $d_\infty$ are **one topological space**, and it is metrizable
   ([[def-metrizable-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** The metric $d_\infty$ is a maximum over $n$ terms, which does
not exist for $n = 0$; [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries the same hypothesis, and it
is carried here for the same reason. For $n = 0$ the product is a one-point space
and there is nothing to compare.

Let $n\ge1$. The set $\mathbb Q^n$ is countable and dense in $\mathbb R^n$. Moreover the rational open boxes

$$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i),\qquad a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q,\quad a_i<b_i,$$

form a countable basis for the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$.

A topological space $X$ is **second countable** when its topology has a basis $\mathcal B$ that is at most countable ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]], [[def-countable]]). Thus every open set is a union of members of one at most countable family $\mathcal B$.

Let $M$ be a topological $n$-manifold ([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]).
A **chart** on $M$ is a pair $(U,\varphi)$ in which:

- $U\subseteq M$ is open, called the **coordinate domain**;
- $\varphi:U\to\widehat U$ is a homeomorphism onto an open subset
  $\widehat U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]), called
  the **coordinate map**; the open set $\widehat U=\varphi(U)$ is the **chart
  image**.

For $n\ge1$ and $i<n$, the $i$-th **coordinate function** is
$$x^i:=\pi_i\circ\varphi:U\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad x^i(p)=\varphi(p)_i,$$
so that $\varphi=(x^0,\ldots,x^{n-1})$. A chart is often written
$(U,(x^0,\ldots,x^{n-1}))$
and the coordinates are then used to name points of $U$. In dimension zero the
coordinate map is the unique map to $\{0\}$ and there are no coordinate functions.

Let $m\ge1$, let $q\in\mathbb N_0$, let $W\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and
let $f:W\to\mathbb R^q$. The map $f$ is **smooth** (of class $C^\infty$) when
every component $f_l:W\to\mathbb R$, $l<q$, is of class $C^k$ for
every $k\in\mathbb N$, where scalar
$C^k$ means that every iterated coordinate derivative through order $k$ exists
and is continuous on $W$ ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).
For $m=0$ the domain is the one-point space or the empty set and every map from
it is declared smooth; for $q=0$ there are no components and every map into the
one-point space is smooth.

Let $M$ be a topological $n$-manifold and let $(U,\varphi)$ and $(V,\psi)$ be
charts on $M$ ([[def-manifold-chart-coordinate-domain-and-coordinate-functions]]).
The charts are **smoothly compatible** when $U\cap V=\varnothing$, or when
$n\ge1$ and both **transition maps**

$$\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U\cap V)\longrightarrow\psi(U\cap V), \qquad \varphi\circ\psi^{-1}:\psi(U\cap V)\longrightarrow\varphi(U\cap V)$$

are smooth in the sense above. Both directions of the transition are part of the
definition; in dimension zero overlapping charts have the same one-point image,
the only transition is the identity, and overlapping charts are declared
compatible.

Let $M$ be a topological $n$-manifold. A **smooth atlas** on $M$ is a family
$\mathcal A=(U_i,\varphi_i)_{i\in I}$ of charts on $M$
([[def-manifold-chart-coordinate-domain-and-coordinate-functions]]) such that:

1. the coordinate domains cover $M$, that is $\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i=M$; and
2. any two members of $\mathcal A$ are smoothly compatible
   ([[def-smoothly-compatible-charts]]).

Two atlases $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ on $M$ are **compatible** when every
chart of $\mathcal A$ is smoothly compatible with every chart of $\mathcal B$.
The family of all charts of both atlases is written $\mathcal A\cup\mathcal B$.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a smooth atlas on a topological manifold $M$, with generated
smooth structure $[\mathcal A]$.

1. $[\mathcal A]$ is a smooth atlas containing $\mathcal A$, and it is maximal:
   every smooth atlas on $M$ that contains $[\mathcal A]$ equals $[\mathcal A]$.
2. For a second smooth atlas $\mathcal B$ on $M$, the two generated structures
   coincide, $[\mathcal A]=[\mathcal B]$, if and only if
   $\mathcal A\cup\mathcal B$ is a smooth atlas.
3. Consequently $\mathcal A$ is contained in exactly one maximal smooth atlas,
   namely $[\mathcal A]$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be linear. It is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$S:W\to V$ such that

$$S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_V,\qquad T\circ S=\operatorname{id}_W.$$

Such an $S$ is the **inverse linear map** of $T$, denoted $T^{-1}$. The two
inverse equations make $T$ bijective and determine $T^{-1}$ uniquely. An
invertible linear map is also called a **linear isomorphism**, and $V$ and $W$
are **linearly isomorphic**, written $V\cong W$, when such a map exists.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. Then $W$ is a smooth
$n$-manifold: the one-chart atlas $\{(W,\mathrm{id}_W)\}$ is a smooth atlas, and the
smooth structure it generates is the one induced on the open subset $W$ of
$\mathbb R^n$. A chart $(U,\varphi)$ on $W$ belongs to this structure exactly
when both transition maps between $\varphi$ and the identity are smooth, that
is, exactly when $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ and its inverse are smooth as maps
between Euclidean open sets.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds. A **diffeomorphism** from $M$ to $N$ is a
bijective smooth map $F:M\to N$ whose inverse $F^{-1}:N\to M$ is smooth. Since
a bijective smooth map and its smooth inverse are both continuous
([[prop-smooth-maps-are-continuous]]), every diffeomorphism is a homeomorphism,
but the converse fails. The manifolds $M$ and $N$ are **diffeomorphic**, written
$M\cong N$, when a diffeomorphism $M\to N$ exists.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map. Then $F$ is a **local diffeomorphism** when
every $p\in M$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq M$ such that $F(U)$ is
open in $N$ and the corestriction $F|_{U}^{F(U)}:U\to F(U)$ is a
diffeomorphism onto the open submanifold $F(U)$
([[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]]).

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

derivations.claim: The chart $x$ is a bijection $A\to\mathbb R^4$ by [L1]. Its preimages of Euclidean open sets form a topology: preimages preserve arbitrary unions and finite intersections and carry $\varnothing,\mathbb R^4$ to $\varnothing,A$, respectively, so [L3] applies. By the definition of this transported topology $x^{-1}(V)$ is open in $A$ for every open $V\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ while $(x^{-1})^{-1}(U)=x(U)$ is open in $\mathbb R^4$ for every open $U\subseteq A$; hence $x$ and $x^{-1}$ are continuous by [L2], so $x$ is a homeomorphism [L2], and the transported topology is the unique topology for which this holds, its open sets being exactly the preimages of the open sets of $\mathbb R^4$ [L2, L3].

Let $N$ be an invertible real $4\times4$ matrix and $c\in\mathbb R^4$, and put $g(u):=Nu+c$. Then $g$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse $g^{-1}(w)=N^{-1}(w-c)$ by [L16]. Each component is $g_l(u)=\sum_jN_{lj}u_j+c_l$; by the definition of the partial derivative [L14], $\partial_jg_l(a)=N_{lj}$ for every $a$, a constant function, and every iterated partial derivative of order at least $2$ is the partial derivative of a constant, hence exists and equals $0$; therefore each component is of class $C^k$ for every $k$ by [L14], so $g$ is smooth by [L11]. Moreover $g$ and $g^{-1}$ are continuous: $\lvert(Nx)_l\rvert\le(\max_j\lvert x_j\rvert)\sum_j\lvert N_{lj}\rvert\le\lVert x\rVert_2\sum_j\lvert N_{lj}\rvert$ by [L15], so $\lVert g(u)-g(v)\rVert_2=\lVert N(u-v)\rVert_2\le K_N\lVert u-v\rVert_2$ with $K_N:=\bigl(\sum_l(\sum_j\lvert N_{lj}\rvert)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$, which is the Lipschitz condition giving the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition of continuity, and the same estimate with $N^{-1}$ in place of $N$ applies to $g^{-1}$.

$\mathbb R^4$ with its standard topology is metrizable by [L7], so distinct points of $\mathbb R^4$ have disjoint open neighbourhoods by [L6]. For $p
e q$ in $A$ the points $x(p)
e x(q)$ are distinct because $x$ is injective by step 1.1; choosing disjoint open sets $V
i x(p)$ and $W
i x(q)$ in $\mathbb R^4$, the preimages $x^{-1}(V)$ and $x^{-1}(W)$ are open in $A$ by step 1.1 and are disjoint, so $A$ is Hausdorff by [L5].

The rational open boxes form a countable basis $\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb R^4$ by [L8]. The family $\{x^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal B\}$ is countable and consists of open subsets of $A$ by step 1.1; and it is a basis for the transported topology: if $U\subseteq A$ is open, then $x(U)$ is open in $\mathbb R^4$ by step 1.1 and equals the union of the members of $\mathcal B$ contained in it, so $U$ is the union of the corresponding sets $x^{-1}(B)$, each open in $A$. Hence $A$ is second countable by [L9].

Let $y(p)=Mx(p)+b$ with $M$ invertible and $b\in\mathbb R^4$, and put $g(u):=Mu+b$. Then $y=g\circ x$ is a bijection $A\to\mathbb R^4$ by steps 1.1 and 1.2; it is continuous because for open $V\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ the preimage $y^{-1}(V)=x^{-1}(g^{-1}(V))$ is open in $A$ by steps 1.1 and 1.2; and $y^{-1}$ is continuous because for open $U\subseteq A$ its preimage under $y^{-1}$ is $y(U)=g(x(U))$, open in $\mathbb R^4$ by steps 1.1 and 1.2. Thus $y$ is a homeomorphism onto $\mathbb R^4$.

Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame with chart $x'$. By the transition law of [L1], $x'=M^{-1}\bigl(x-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x+b$ with $b:=-M^{-1}x(o')$, where $M$ is the change-of-basis matrix between the two ordered bases and $M^{-1}$ is invertible because both families are ordered bases; this exhibits $x'$ as an affine chart with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ in the sense of the affine maps of step 1.2.

By step 2.1 the space $A$ is Hausdorff and by step 2.2 it is second countable. It is locally Euclidean of dimension $4$: for every $p\in A$ the whole space $A$ is an open neighbourhood of $p$ by [L3], and $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a homeomorphism onto the open subset $\mathbb R^4\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ by step 1.1. Hence $A$ is a topological $4$-manifold by [L4], proving claim 1; the homeomorphisms $x$ and $y$ established in steps 1.1 and 2.3 are therefore charts by [L10].

The transition map between the charts $(A,x)$ and $(A,y)$ of step 2.3 is $y\circ x^{-1}=g$, and its inverse transition is $x\circ y^{-1}=g^{-1}$; by step 1.2 both are smooth, so the two charts are smoothly compatible by [L11].

Let $x'$ be another inertial chart, written $x'=g'\circ x$ with $g'$ an affine map of $\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part by step 2.4. For a subset $U\subseteq A$, openness in the topology transported by $x'$ means that $x'(U)=g'(x(U))$ is open in $\mathbb R^4$, which by step 1.2 (a homeomorphism maps open sets to open sets and reflects them) is equivalent to $x(U)$ being open in $\mathbb R^4$, that is, to $U$ being open in the topology transported by $x$ by step 1.1. Hence the two transported topologies coincide.

The pair $(A,x)$ is a chart by steps 1.1 and [L10]; the one-chart family $\{(A,x)\}$ covers $A$ and its sole transition $x\circ x^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R^4}$ is smooth by step 1.2, so it is a smooth atlas by [L12]; the maximal smooth atlas it generates exists and is unique by [L13], and $A$ with this smooth structure is a smooth $4$-manifold by [L12].

Every affine chart $y=Mx+b$ is smoothly compatible with the chart $(A,x)$ by step 3.2, and every inertial chart is an affine chart by step 2.4; hence each of these charts belongs to the smooth structure generated by the atlas $\{(A,x)\}$ of step 4.1, by the criterion of [L13] that two one-chart atlases generate the same structure exactly when their union is a smooth atlas.

$\mathbb R^4$ is an open subset of itself and carries the standard smooth structure generated by the one-chart atlas $\{(\mathbb R^4,\mathrm{id})\}$ by [L17]. With respect to the charts $(A,x)$ of step 4.1 and $(\mathbb R^4,\mathrm{id})$, the coordinate representative of $x$ is $\mathrm{id}\circ x\circ x^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R^4}$ and the representative of $x^{-1}$ is likewise $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R^4}$; the identity of $\mathbb R^4$ has components $u_l$ whose partial derivatives are the constants $\delta_{lj}$ with all higher iterated partial derivatives $0$, so it is smooth by [L14] and [L11]. Hence $x$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse, that is, a diffeomorphism $A\to\mathbb R^4$ by [L18], proving claim 2.

The smooth structures generated by the one-chart atlases $\{(A,x)\}$ and $\{(A,x')\}$ of two inertial charts coincide: by step 2.4 and step 5.1 the chart $x'$ is smoothly compatible with $x$, so the union of the two one-chart atlases is a smooth atlas and [L13] gives equality of the generated maximal atlases; combined with step 3.3 this proves claim 3 for the transition and claim 4.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with its inertial chart
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Every $v\in V$ has a unique
coordinate vector $(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ with $v=\sum_av^ae_a$. For an ordered
$4$-tuple $(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ of vectors of $V$ let

$$[v_j^a]:=\begin{pmatrix}v_0^0&v_1^0&v_2^0&v_3^0\\ v_0^1&v_1^1&v_2^1&v_3^1\\ v_0^2&v_1^2&v_2^2&v_3^2\\ v_0^3&v_1^3&v_2^3&v_3^3\end{pmatrix}$$

be the $4\times4$ real matrix whose $j$-th column lists the coordinates of
$v_j$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, and define

$$\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3):=\det\bigl([v_j^a]\bigr)$$

by the determinant of a square matrix
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]). Then $\epsilon$ is an **alternating
$4$-linear form** on $V$
([[def-alternating-k-linear-map]]): the determinant is multilinear and
alternating in the columns, so replacing one $v_j$ by $\lambda v_j+\mu w$
replaces the $j$-th column correspondingly and $\epsilon$ is linear in each
argument, and $\epsilon(v_0,\ldots,v_3)=0$ whenever two arguments coincide,
since then two columns coincide
([[thm-determinant-is-the-unique-normalized-alternating-multilinear-function]]).
The form $\epsilon$ is the **oriented volume form of the model**. Its
well-definedness as a form of the model, independent of the inertial frame used
in the display, is proved in [[lem-volume-form-is-independent-of-the-oriented-frame]].

**Components.** Write $\epsilon_{abcd}:=\epsilon(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$ for the
components of $\epsilon$ in the inertial frame. Evaluating the determinant on
the coordinate matrix of $(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$, which is the permutation matrix
of the tuple, gives

$$\epsilon_{0123}=+1,\qquad \epsilon_{abcd}=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\ \text{ if }(a,b,c,d)=(\sigma(0),\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\sigma(3))\ \text{ for a permutation }\sigma,$$

and $\epsilon_{abcd}=0$ whenever two of the indices coincide; these are the
**permutation symbols** of the frame. Indeed the coordinate vector of $e_a$ is
the $a$-th standard basis vector, so the coordinate matrix of
$(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$ is the permutation matrix of the tuple and its determinant
is $+1$ on the identity tuple, the sign of the permutation otherwise, and $0$
when two indices repeat.

**Raised components.** The **inverse metric** $\eta^{ab}$ is the inverse of the
matrix $\eta_{ab}:=\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, which
exists because $\eta$ is nondegenerate
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]); it is again
$\eta^{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)^{ab}$. The raised components of the
volume form are

$$\epsilon^{abcd}:=\eta^{aa'}\eta^{bb'}\eta^{cc'}\eta^{dd'}\epsilon_{a'b'c'd'}$$

(summation over repeated primed indices). Since the inverse metric is diagonal
with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$, only one term contributes to $\epsilon^{0123}$
and

$$\epsilon^{0123}=\eta^{00}\eta^{11}\eta^{22}\eta^{33}\epsilon_{0123}=(-1)(+1)(+1)(+1)(+1)=-1 .$$

**Spatial symbol.** The **spatial permutation symbol** $\epsilon_{ijk}$ for
$i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$ is defined by $\epsilon_{123}=+1$ together with alternation
in the three indices; explicitly $\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ for even permutations of
$(1,2,3)$, $\epsilon_{ijk}=-1$ for odd permutations, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$
whenever two of $i,j,k$ coincide.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $\eta$ be a Lorentz form on a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$. There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$. Such a basis
is called **$\eta$-orthonormal**; in every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis
exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the
count is the inertia $(3,1,0)$ of $\eta$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space ([[def-dimension]]). Two ordered bases $\mathcal B,\mathcal B'$ of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) are declared **equivalent** when the determinant of the unique change-of-basis linear isomorphism $P:V\to V$ carrying $\mathcal B$ to $\mathcal B'$ satisfies $\det P>0$, where the determinant is [[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]] and positivity is the order of the real field [[thm-reals-ordered-field]].

**This is an equivalence relation.** The identity change of basis has determinant $1>0$. If $\mathcal B\sim\mathcal B'$ through $P$, then $\mathcal B'\sim\mathcal B$ through $P^{-1}$, and $\det(P^{-1})=(\det P)^{-1}>0$. If $\mathcal B\sim\mathcal B'\sim\mathcal B''$ through $P,Q$, then $\det(Q\circ P)=\det Q\det P>0$ by [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]].

An **orientation** of $V$ is an equivalence class of ordered bases under this relation; a basis in the chosen class is **positively oriented** for that orientation. When $\dim V\ge1$ there are exactly two orientations: fixing one ordered basis $\mathcal B_0$, every other basis $\mathcal B$ has $\det P>0$ or $\det P<0$ by the trichotomy of [[thm-reals-ordered-field]]. If $\dim V=1$, replacing the sole basis vector of $\mathcal B_0$ by its negative produces a basis with determinant $-1$; if $\dim V\ge2$, interchanging two entries of $\mathcal B_0$ does the same. Thus both classes occur. When $\dim V=0$ the only ordered basis is the empty one and there is exactly one orientation.

Let $F$ be a field and let $V,W$ be $F$-vector spaces ([[def-vector-space]]). For $k\ge0$, a map

$$f:V^k\longrightarrow W$$

is **$k$-linear** (multilinear) when it is linear in each of its $k$ arguments separately, with the other arguments held fixed. It is **alternating** when

$$f(v_1,\ldots,v_k)=0\qquad\text{whenever }v_i=v_j\text{ for some }1\le i<j\le k.$$

Let $\eta$ be a Lorentz form on a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$. There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$. Such a basis
is called **$\eta$-orthonormal**; in every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis
exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the
count is the inertia $(3,1,0)$ of $\eta$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are

ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a

component condition is vacuous.

derivations.claim: Fix $v\in V$ and a smooth germ $[f]$ at $p$. By [L6] the curve $c(t):=p+tv$ has coordinate representation $x(c(t))=x(p)+tu$ with $u=E^{-1}(v)$, a smooth curve in $\mathbb R^4$; hence $c$ is a smooth curve through $p$ in the chart $x$, and $t\mapsto f(c(t))$ is smooth near $0$ by [L2], so its derivative at $0$ exists. If $g$ agrees with $f$ near $p$, then $f\circ c$ and $g\circ c$ agree near $0$, so the derivative depends only on the germ $[f]$; hence $\Phi_p(v)([f])$ is a well-defined real number.

With $u=E^{-1}(v)=(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$, set $F:=f\circ x^{-1}$, the smooth coordinate representative of $[f]$ near $x(p)$ [L2]. Then $f(c(t))=F(x(p)+tu)$ for $t$ near $0$, so by the chain rule [L4] applied to $t\mapsto x(p)+tu$ and to $F$, whose total derivative at $x(p)$ has matrix the Jacobian by [L3], $\Phi_p(v)([f])=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\bigr|_0F\bigl(x(p)+tu\bigr)=D F(x(p))\cdot u=\sum_{a=0}^3u^a\partial_aF(x(p))$.
$\Phi_p$ is linear in $v$: by step 2.1 the value $\Phi_p(v)([f])=\sum_au^a\partial_aF(x(p))$ is a linear function of $u=E^{-1}(v)$, and $E^{-1}$ is linear by [L6].

$\Phi_p(v)$ is a derivation at $p$: it is $\mathbb R$-linear in the germ because the sum and scalar-multiple derivative rules of [L7] apply to $t\mapsto f(p+tv)$ near $0$. For smooth germs $[f],[g]$, the coordinate representatives satisfy $((fg)\circ x^{-1})=(f\circ x^{-1})(g\circ x^{-1})$, so the one-variable product rule [L7] applied to the differentiable functions $t\mapsto F(y+t\mathbf e_a)$ and $t\mapsto G(y+t\mathbf e_a)$, where $y=x(p)\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\mathbf e_a\in\mathbb R^4$ is the $a$-th standard coordinate vector gives the product rule for the partial derivatives: $\partial_a((fg)\circ x^{-1})(x(p))=f(p)\partial_a(g\circ x^{-1})(x(p))+g(p)\partial_a(f\circ x^{-1})(x(p))$, since $f(x^{-1}(x(p)))=f(p)$ and likewise for $g$; substituting into step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(v)([f][g])=f(p)\Phi_p(v)([g])+g(p)\Phi_p(v)([f])$, so $\Phi_p(v)\in T_pA$ by [L1].

$\Phi_p$ is injective: suppose $\Phi_p(v)=0$ with coordinate vector $u=E^{-1}(v)$. Applying $\Phi_p(v)$ to the germ of the coordinate function $x^a$ gives, by step 2.1, $\Phi_p(v)([x^a])=\sum_bu^b\partial_b(x^a\circ x^{-1})(x(p))=\sum_bu^b\delta^a_b=u^a$; hence $u=0$, and since $E^{-1}$ is injective by [L6], $v=0$.

$\Phi_p$ carries the basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ to the coordinate derivations: for $v=e_a$ one has $u=E^{-1}(e_a)=(\delta^a_b)_b$ by [L6], so step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(e_a)([f])=\partial_aF(x(p))=\partial_a|_p([f])$ for every smooth germ, that is, $\Phi_p(e_a)=\partial_a|_p$. By [L5] the derivations $\partial_a|_p$ form a basis of $T_pA$, so the linear map $\Phi_p$ carries a basis of $V$ to a basis of $T_pA$; hence $\Phi_p$ is surjective (its image contains a basis) and injective by step 3.3, so it is a linear isomorphism $V\to T_pA$.

Finally, let $v=\sum_av^ae_a$; then $u=E^{-1}(v)=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$, so step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(v)([f])=\sum_av^a\partial_aF(x(p))$, that is, $\Phi_p(v)=\sum_av^a\partial_a|_p$.
